edges.description: Deposited bacteria must secure host iron to expand from the inoculation site.
Expanded bacterial populations must withstand complement and serum killing to disseminate through blood.
In foodborne disease, serum-resistant organisms that expand in the gut can breach the epithelial barrier.
In wound disease, serum-resistant organisms that expand in skin and fascia deliver cytolytic and proteolytic virulence factors.
Epithelial barrier disruption in the gut produces the gastroenteritis syndrome of foodborne V. vulnificus infection.
Barrier failure allows enteric bacteria to disseminate systemically and trigger innate inflammatory sepsis.
Cytolysin-driven cell injury underlies the rapidly progressive soft-tissue inflammation of wound disease.
Cytolytic and microvascular injury produces the hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions characteristic of this organism.
Microvascular injury accompanying cytolysin activity causes hemorrhagic skin lesions.
Soft-tissue cytotoxicity allows the organism to enter blood and seed fatal systemic inflammation.
Protease-driven tissue destruction underlies the necrotizing wound syndrome requiring surgical source control.
Protease-mediated tissue breakdown permits systemic spread and inflammation.
Systemic inflammatory activation manifests clinically as sepsis.
The cytokine cascade drives vasodilatory septic shock with hypotension.
Oysters and warm seawater carry the organism to the gut or directly into wounded skin.

nodes.description: Encapsulated opaque V. vulnificus cells produce capsular polysaccharide that protects the bacterium from normal human serum, enabling survival during bloodstream spread.

evidence.reference_title: Capsular polysaccharide production and serum survival of Vibrio vulnificus are dependent on antitermination control by RfaH.
evidence.snippet: the rfaH mutant produced negligible CPS and was highly sensitive to killing by normal human serum, results which indicate that RfaH is likely essential for virulence in this bacterium.

nodes.description: Disseminated invasive infection elicits high TNF-alpha, interleukin-1 beta, and IL-6 responses that track with fatality in experimental infection and clinically appear as sepsis, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multiorgan dysfunction.

evidence.reference_title: Synergistic antimicrobial effect of cefotaxime and minocycline on proinflammatory cytokine levels in a murine model of Vibrio vulnificus infection.
evidence.snippet: Serum levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin (IL)-1 beta, and IL-6 post-infection were found to be inoculum dose-dependent and positively correlated to the subsequent fatality rate in the infected mice.

nodes.description: Severe suspected V. vulnificus infection is treated urgently with active combination antibiotics, classically a third-generation cephalosporin plus a tetracycline.

evidence.reference_title: In vitro synergism between cefotaxime and minocycline against Vibrio vulnificus.
evidence.snippet: We conclude that cefotaxime and minocycline acted synergistically in inhibiting V. vulnificus in vitro.

evidence.snippet: A multidisciplinary treatment protocol for necrotizing fasciitis caused by V. vulnificus was developed in our institute, namely, ceftriaxone or ceftazidime combined with doxycycline or minocycline followed by an emergency fasciotomy and intensive care unit admission.

nodes.description: During intragastric infection, the RtxA1 MARTX toxin forms membrane pores and translocates effector domains into intestinal epithelial cells, disrupting epithelial barrier function before overt cell lysis and enabling dissemination from the gut.

evidence.reference_title: The Effector Domain Region of the Vibrio vulnificus MARTX Toxin Confers Biphasic Epithelial Barrier Disruption and Is Essential for Systemic Spread from the Intestine.
evidence.snippet: The MARTX effector domain region is essential for bacterial dissemination from the intestine, but dissemination occurs in the absence of overt intestinal tissue pathology.

nodes.description: Eating contaminated oysters introduces V. vulnificus to the intestine, whereas direct marine-water contact inoculates wounded skin and subcutaneous tissue.
